newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia weighs strike's potential economic impact.
newsitem.headline: Colombia weighs strike's potential economic impact.

text.p: Colombia's airports, telecommunications and oil sector seem set to be the first casualties of the looming national strike due to begin at the stroke of midnight (12 a.m. EST/0500 GMT Tuesday), industrialists and union officials said on Monday.

The indefinite stoppage declared by about 800,000 state workers is not expected to have an immediate impact on the coffee industry or on the road transport sector, which accounts for over 95 percent of domestic cargo shipments.
But exporters said they feared the strike could hit customs operations and hold up shipments from some ports -- claims rejected by customs and excise tax officials.
Union leaders say they will keep workers off their jobs until their demands for salary increases and labor policy are met.
A spokeswoman for state-run oil company Ecopetrol said the main petroleum problems with the strike were likely to occur in the oil production center of Barrancabermeja in central Colombia.
She was unable to say immediately if refining, pumping and production operations would be suspended.

Gustavo Triana, a leader of the main oil workers' union USO, leader said: "We are not announcing exactly what measures we will be taking nor the magnitude of our action but it is fair to say that whole areas of the state oil industry will be paralyzed,"

Earlier in the day Monday, Oscar Garcia, head of the Colombian Airport Technicians Association, said ITS members would join the strike. The technicians are responsible for maintaining air transport communication systems, radars and navigation equipment in all the country's airports, including the major international facilities in Bogota, Cali and Medellin.

Air traffic controllers will operate as normal, said Cesar Valle, one of the heads of the Air Traffic Controllers Association, but he added the action by technicians will lead to "inevitable" delays on all national and international flights.
Those delays will be between one and two hours, Valle said, and toward Tuesday afternoon and evening the backlog of delayed flights may lead to some cancelations.
Initial fears that Colombia may be isolated from the outside world as a result of action by workers of the state phone company Telecom, as in 1993, appear to have receded.
Phone workers' union leader Eberto Lpez said a "minimum service" would be maintained. All operator services will be suspended but direct dial calls can still be made, he said.
Much of the Colombia's public administration is set to be paralyzed by the indefinite strike, rasing concern among some coffee exporters that shipments could be delayed.

A spokesman at the main Pacific coast port of Buenaventura -- a private facility -- through which about 60 percent of the volume of Colombia's exports pass, did not foresee any direct implications of the state workers' strike on port activities.
Most transport services across the country are run by private operators and Jairo Tafur, of the Colombian Truck Drivers' Association said the strike would not have a direct effect on road freight.

However, he said if striking workers blocked roads or if leftist guerrillas threatened attacks on long-distance trucks as they have in the past, then transport services could be delayed or even halted.
